title: Whats in Your Way
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article offers a structured approach to the leadership conversation about obstacles, breaking constraints into three categories: structural issues built into the organization, obstacles created by the leader's own behavior, and obstacles that are largely self-manufactured by the team member. Specific example questions are provided for each category, including the pointed 'What do I do that makes your work more difficult than it should be?' The author notes these conversations matter even when a leader can't fix a given constraint, since simply discussing it builds trust and connection. The piece closes emphasizing that top performers don't let obstacles define what's possible.
points: Obstacle conversations work best when broken into three categories: structural issues, leader-caused obstacles, and self-manufactured constraints.
Leaders should be willing to ask directly what they themselves do that makes a team member's work harder.
Even when a leader can't fix a given obstacle, discussing it openly builds trust and connection with the team member.
Specific example questions are provided for surfacing each category of obstacle.
quotes: Good leaders do everything in their power to remove obstacles that prevent team members from being the most productive they can be.
There may be structural issues inherent to the team or organization that get in the way.
Usually, one of the biggest impediments to productivity team members face is the leader.
Asking, “What do I do that makes your work more difficult than it should be?” or “What could I do to make your job or work much easier?” will also open up the conversation.
This question often jars a team member and gets them to honestly reflect on their role and accountability in addressing their own productivity.
Top performers never allow what they can’t do to thwart what they can do.
